reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A focal dystonia causing involuntary, bilateral, and usually symmetric contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles, producing forced eye closure
It typically begins in adults, more often women, with increased blinking and eye irritation before progressing to sustained spasms of closure
Symptoms are frequently aggravated by bright light, stress, reading, or driving and may be temporarily relieved by sensory tricks (geste antagoniste) such as touching the face
Severe cases cause functional blindness because the eyes cannot be kept open, despite intact vision
It may occur in isolation or as part of a segmental dystonia such as Meige syndrome, which combines blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia
Secondary causes, including drug-induced dystonia and ocular surface disease that provokes reflex closure, should be considered before diagnosing the primary form
It is distinguished from hemifacial spasm, which is unilateral and involves the whole hemiface, and from ptosis and eyelid apraxia
Botulinum toxin injection into the periocular muscles is the mainstay of treatment, with oral medication and surgery in selected refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Blepharospasm is a focal cranial dystonia in which abnormal function of basal ganglia and brainstem circuits controlling blink and eyelid movement leads to excessive, involuntary orbicularis oculi contraction. Reduced inhibition within the blink reflex pathway and abnormal sensorimotor integration are implicated, and dopaminergic and other neurotransmitter systems are thought to be involved. Ocular surface irritation can trigger or worsen symptoms through the reflex arc, and the disorder can extend to adjacent facial and jaw muscles in segmental forms.
additionalDifferentials: Ocular surface disease causing reflex blinking (dry eye, blepharitis)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment to distinguish from hemifacial spasm, apraxia, and ocular surface disease
Ophthalmological examination for dry eye and other irritative causes
Medication review to identify drug-induced dystonia
Neurological evaluation for associated dystonia (Meige syndrome) or other signs
Brain imaging when secondary or atypical features are present
redFlags: Additional neurological signs suggesting a broader neurodegenerative or structural disorder
Recent exposure to dopamine-blocking or other causative drugs
Rapidly progressive or strictly unilateral involvement prompting reconsideration
Functional visual impairment from inability to open the eyes
reference.prognosis: Blepharospasm is usually chronic and can fluctuate but is not life-threatening; most patients gain substantial and repeatable relief from botulinum toxin, though the condition generally requires ongoing treatment.
pitfalls: Overlooking treatable ocular surface disease driving reflex eye closure
Misdiagnosing unilateral hemifacial spasm as blepharospasm
Failing to identify drug-induced dystonia from a reversible cause
Missing associated oromandibular dystonia in Meige syndrome
management: Botulinum toxin injection into the orbicularis oculi as first-line treatment, repeated at regular intervals
Treat coexisting ocular surface irritation with lubricants for dry eye, and reduce photophobia with tinted (FL-41) lenses
Review and withdraw dopamine-blocking or other offending drugs where the dystonia is drug-induced
Adjunctive oral agents such as anticholinergics, benzodiazepines or baclofen for inadequate response to injections
Orbicularis myectomy for botulinum-resistant cases, with deep brain stimulation considered in severe segmental or generalised dystonia (Meige syndrome)
Ongoing neurology and movement-disorder follow-up with reassessment of dose and treatment response
